what_happened: The person running Athena rewrote a "keep the batch running" request so it covered only items the scope guard had paused. They did this without checking the other ways a repeatedly failing item can stop a batch. At 11:13pm UTC an item was flagged after two failures instead of being paused. The narrowed request did not cover that, so the batch stopped again while money and slots were still available. This is an intervention note, not a failed job record.
cause: Athena does not list the states in which a failing item can halt a drain: paused, flagged, failed and others. A request that fixes drain-stopping behaviour is therefore written from memory of one path. Nothing compares the request's scope with the code's real set of stop outcomes, and nothing warns the writer that the request is partial. The gap shows only when the next item stops the batch by a different route. This is the same urgent-unblocking-fix problem as the earlier case. That request was too wide to finish. This one was too narrow to work. In both, the request's size and coverage are not checked against the code before it is queued.
prevention: Add a check that runs when a drain-continuation request is read or planned. It lists every outcome that makes the drain stop on an item (pause, flag, fail, hold and so on), taken from the code. It requires each outcome to be handled by the request or named as out of scope. It also requires a test that drives an item to each outcome and shows the drain continues. Until then, the default is that an unblocking request states the outcome as "the drain continues past any item that stops it" and does not name a single case.
proposed_request: Make the queue drain continue past any item that fails repeatedly, whatever state that leaves it in. Outcome: when an item ends paused by the scope guard, flagged after repeated failures, or failed, the drain skips it, records why, and takes the next runnable item while budget and slots remain. The drain stops only when nothing runnable is left, or the budget or slots run out. Acceptance: (1) the code has one place that lists every state in which an item can stop a drain, and a test fails if a new state is added without being handled there; (2) tests drive an item into the paused state, into the flagged-after-two-failures state, and into the failed state, and in each case the drain goes on to the next item; (3) skipped items appear in the drain summary with their state and reason; (4) the change is one job and does not add failure-cause sorting.
